I am playing Monopoly as player p4.

I have $870 and am on ILLINOIS_AVENUE. My holdings include Mediterranean, Electric Company, St. James Place, Tennessee Avenue, Kentucky Avenue, Indiana Avenue, and Boardwalk. The orange monopoly is incomplete because two of those properties are mortgaged, so I cannot build houses there. I need to decide which single action to take.

The yellow monopoly is complete with one house on each property. Water Works and Boardwalk are mortgaged, so dark blue cannot be built on. I have two get-out-of-jail-free cards. The opponent has $507 and is on ATLANTIC_AVENUE.

The opponent owns Baltic, all light blues with hotels, all pinks with four houses, all greens with four houses, and all four railroads. Players one and two are bankrupt, so this is a one-on-one game. I am calculating my available cash and sellable assets to plan a winning move.

Emergency liquidity totals roughly $1,400 from cash, house sales, and mortgages. The opponent's light blue hotels are the biggest immediate threat, with rents of $550 to $600.

The opponent's four-house pinks and greens are also dangerous, with rents up to $1,200. However, the bank only has five houses left, so they cannot hotel their greens or pinks without selling existing houses first.

The opponent can upgrade their greens to hotels for $200 each. With $507 cash, they could afford two hotels and still have $107 left. I had passed on my turn while they were building.

I am now deciding my post-turn action. The opponent is on Atlantic Avenue, and the yellow monopoly rent with one house there is $130.

I am weighing whether to build two houses on each yellow property. That would cost $450 and leave me with $420 cash, satisfying the even-build rule.

I can build five more houses for $750, leaving $120 cash. The even-distribution rule allows a 3/3/2 split from the current 1/1/1 layout. Rent would rise to $900 on Atlantic and Ventnor, and $1,000 on Marvin.

The key strategic question is whether I can force the opponent to sell their expensive houses. Selling a hotel returns four houses to the bank at half price. This creates a complex chain of potential downsizing.

I am reconsidering whether to build houses. Five yellow houses cost $750 and would leave me with roughly $1,045 in cash. That is still below the opponent's building equity. A single roll of two from Atlantic Avenue lands on Ventnor, which carries only one house and costs $130. That is not enough to force the opponent to sell their expensive properties.

From Atlantic Avenue, the opponent can land on Ventnor for $130, Marvin Gardens for $150, or Park Place for $35. A roll of five sends them to jail. All other outcomes are either neutral or their own properties.

Building one more house on each yellow property would cost $450 and leave me with $420. The opponent could still pay the resulting $390 or $450 rent without selling any buildings. To force them to sell, I would need to build five houses for $750, leaving only $120 cash. That would raise rent to $900 or $1,000, which they cannot afford without liquidating their expensive properties.

Selling a hotel returns only four houses at half price, so that path is too slow. Five green houses sell for $500, which covers the roughly $493 shortfall. This confirms that forcing the opponent to strip their greens is feasible.

Selling evenly across monopolies means stripping one house from each property at a time. Dropping the opponent's greens from four houses to two would cost $600, leaving them with $500 to $550 rent on Pacific, North Carolina, and Pennsylvania. Their pink houses sell for $50 each, so twelve of them total $600.

Selling all twelve pink houses raises $600, giving the opponent $1,107 in cash. They can then pay a $1,000 rent without selling any green houses. A single large hit therefore cannot force them to strip their greens. I am now considering whether a larger rent would change this.

The bank only holds five houses, so I cannot build hotels. The best I can do is three houses on Marvin for $1,000, or three on two properties and two on the third. That still does not force the opponent to strip their greens.

Stripping the opponent's pink monopoly would be valuable. Their four-house pinks are lethal, but once sold, base rents drop to negligible levels. The opponent can raise enough cash by selling just three houses from each pink property to cover a $900 rent on Ventnor. This makes forcing a pink strip a viable strategy.

Dropping the opponent's pink houses to one each would slash their rent from $750 to about $80. I am now weighing whether the $750 build cost is worth it, since the houses can be sold back if I need cash.

Selling the five new houses would return $600, giving total liquidity of roughly $1,025. That is still below the opponent's four-house green rent of about $1,200. Without building, current liquidity of $1,400 covers one green hit but not two or a hotel. The $750 build leaves me slightly more exposed than before.

Building five houses leaves me with only $1,025 in total liquidity. That is below the $1,100 needed to survive a single four-house green rent. I have no other properties to mortgage, so I would be bankrupt if I land on a green. This makes the build a suicide move.

From Illinois Avenue, eleven of the twelve possible rolls land on either my own properties or the opponent's monopolies. Three of those eleven spaces are greens with four houses: Pacific, North Carolina, and Pennsylvania. That gives roughly a one-in-three chance of landing on a green next turn. Building five houses would leave me with only about $1,025 in liquidity, which is below the $1,100 needed to survive a single green rent. The risk of bankruptcy from that roll is too high to justify the build.

I am now considering whether to unmortgage any properties. Unmortgaging the orange monopolies would cost about $198, but building there would still leave me with insufficient liquidity. The yellow monopolies remain the better target.

I checked the board layout and confirmed the opponent is currently on Atlantic Avenue. The orange monopolies sit behind them, so they cannot land there immediately. This makes un-mortgaging the oranges a poor immediate target.

Unmortgaging the orange monopolies is not worth it. The opponent would roll forward into yellows and greens, so those properties are out of reach for now.

Unmortgaging Boardwalk costs $220. That leaves about $650 to build three houses on the dark blue monopoly. Dark blue rent is high, but the opponent is unlikely to land there from Atlantic Avenue.

Unmortgaging Boardwalk is not worth the liquidity hit. The opponent cannot land on dark blue from Atlantic in one roll. Unmortgaging utilities is also a poor use of cash. Completing both monopolies at once would leave me with a weaker brown set rather than a stronger red one.

The orange monopoly is incomplete because two of those properties are mortgaged, so I cannot build houses there. I need to decide which single action to take.

The yellow monopoly is complete with one house on each property. Water Works and Boardwalk are mortgaged, so dark blue cannot be built on. I have two get-out-of-jail-free cards. The opponent has $507 and is on ATLANTIC_AVENUE.

The opponent owns Baltic, all light blues with hotels, all pinks with four houses, all greens with four houses, and all four railroads. Players one and two are bankrupt, so this is a one-on-one game. I am calculating my available cash and sellable assets to plan a winning move.

Emergency liquidity totals roughly $1,400 from cash, house sales, and mortgages. The opponent's light blue hotels are the biggest immediate threat, with rents of $550 to $600.

The opponent's four-house pinks and greens are also dangerous, with rents up to $1,200. However, the bank only has five houses left, so they cannot hotel their greens or pinks without selling existing houses first.

The opponent can upgrade their greens to hotels for $200 each. With $507 cash, they could afford two hotels and still have $107 left. I had passed on my turn while they were building.

I am now deciding my post-turn action. The opponent is on Atlantic Avenue, and the yellow monopoly rent with one house there is $130.

I am weighing whether to build two houses on each yellow property. That would cost $450 and leave me with $420 cash, satisfying the even-build rule.

I can build five more houses for $750, leaving $120 cash. The even-distribution rule allows a 3/3/2 split from the current 1/1/1 layout. Rent would rise to $900 on Atlantic and Ventnor, and $1,000 on Marvin.

The key strategic question is whether I can force the opponent to sell their expensive houses. Selling a hotel returns four houses to the bank at half price. This creates a complex chain of potential downsizing.

I am reconsidering whether to build houses. Five yellow houses cost $750 and would leave me with roughly $1,045 in cash. That is still below the opponent's building equity. Selling evenly across monopolies means stripping one house from each property at a time. Building five houses would leave me with only about $1,025 in liquidity, which is below the $1,100 needed to survive a single green rent. I checked the board layout and confirmed the opponent is currently on Atlantic Avenue. The orange monopolies sit behind them, so they cannot land there immediately. This makes un-mortgaging the oranges a poor immediate target.

Unmortgaging the orange monopolies is not worth it. The opponent would roll forward into yellows and greens, so those properties are out of reach for now.

Unmortgaging Boardwalk costs $220. That leaves about $650 to build three houses on the dark blue monopoly. Dark blue rent is high, but the opponent is unlikely to land there from Atlantic Avenue.
